lines.text: In January 2025, the head of the most famous AI company in the world posted something strange.
"Insane thing," Sam Altman wrote. "We are currently losing money on OpenAI Pro subscriptions."
The plan cost two hundred dollars a month. And some people used so much that they cost OpenAI more than they paid.
The strangest part? He'd picked the price himself.
But this isn't a story about one plan, or one company.
Behind almost every AI subscription you pay for, there's a quiet bet. A bet that you won't use too much.
Then AI agents arrived. And "too much" stopped meaning what it used to.
This October, the small print changed again.
February 1st, 2023. ChatGPT is barely two months old, and millions of people are already using it.
OpenAI announces a paid version. ChatGPT Plus. Twenty dollars a month.
It's a familiar price. About what people already paid for music or a streaming service.
But AI isn't like streaming.
When one more person watches a film, the film doesn't get more expensive. It's already made.
AI is different. Every answer is made fresh, on chips in a data centre, the moment you ask.
The industry measures that work in tokens. Small pieces of words.
More tokens, more computing. More computing, more cost.
So a flat price is a gamble, a bit like a gym membership. Most people come in a few times. Their money pays for the few who come every day.
However, the AI companies had a second reason to feel safe.
Tokens were getting cheaper. Fast.
The investment firm Andreessen Horowitz measured it. For the same level of ability, the price of AI was falling about ten times every year.
Performance like GPT-3's cost sixty dollars per million tokens in 2021. Three years later, about six cents.
So the plan made sense. Even the heaviest users would get cheaper to serve every year. Time was on their side.
They were right about the price of a word.
They were wrong about how many words we'd want.
December 2024. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Pro. Two hundred dollars a month, ten times the price of Plus.
The selling point was a new kind of model, one that reasons. It thinks through a problem before it answers.
But that thinking is made of tokens too. You never see most of it. Someone still pays for it.
A few weeks later came the post. "People use it much more than we expected."
Then the next shift arrived. Not a smarter chatbot, but an agent.
A chatbot answers one question. An agent takes a whole task, opens files, writes code, tests it, fails, and tries again. On its own.
And at every step it re-reads everything it has done so far. Each lap of the loop costs more than the last.
In April 2025, Anthropic launched its own two-hundred-dollar plan, called Max. Programmers pointed its coding agent, Claude Code, at their projects.
Some of them never turned it off.
In July 2025, Anthropic announced weekly limits. It said some people were running Claude Code "continuously in the background, 24/7."
One user on a two-hundred-dollar plan had used, in Anthropic's words, "tens of thousands" of dollars of model usage.
Anthropic said the new limits would affect fewer than five percent of subscribers.
But from the other side of the counter, it looked different. People had paid for a plan sold as twenty times more usage. Nobody had shown them where the ceiling was.
The companies had a problem. Their best customers were their most expensive ones.
One company tried to fix that quietly.
It did not go quietly.
June 2025. Cursor, one of the most popular AI coding apps, changes its twenty-dollar plan.
Before, you got a set number of requests. Now you get twenty dollars of credit, used up at the price of whichever model you pick.
Heavy users pick the best models. Some burn through the credit in days, then get charged extra.
Developers are furious.
Within weeks the CEO apologises. The changes, he writes, were "not communicated clearly. That's our mistake, and we're sorry." Cursor offers refunds.
However, the lesson the industry took away wasn't to stop charging for heavy use. It was to explain it better. And to move slowly.
April 4th, 2026. Anthropic stops letting subscriptions cover outside agent tools, such as OpenClaw. Those now need separate, pay-as-you-go usage.
Late April. GitHub announces that Copilot is moving to usage-based billing, starting June 1st.
The monthly prices stay the same. But heavy use beyond the allowance is now billed in credits, worth one cent each.
Then, in September, the company that started it all.
OpenAI reopens its two-hundred-dollar Pro plan, and adds a new one at five hundred.
For people already on Pro, the old allowance runs until October 29th. After that, the price stays two hundred dollars. What you get for it goes down.
And the reason OpenAI gives is printed right there on its help page.
The lower allowance is "to reflect our increasingly efficient models."
Read that again.
The models get more efficient, and you get less.
To understand how both can be true, you have to look at the receipt from the other side.

chapters.label: 4 · The Other Side of the Receipt

lines.text: In 2025, OpenAI brought in about thirteen billion dollars. According to reports from its investors, it also burned through about eight billion in cash.
And the spending ahead is far bigger.
In late 2025, Sam Altman said OpenAI had committed to about one-point-four trillion dollars of data centres and computing over eight years.
By February 2026, it had told investors a smaller target. Around six hundred billion by 2030. Still one of the largest spending plans in history.
So here is the paradox.
Every token keeps getting cheaper.
But every task uses more of them. Reasoning models think longer. Agents loop, re-read and retry.
The research firm Gartner has called this the inference paradox: cheaper words, bigger bills.
Which leaves every AI company with three choices. Raise the price. Cut what's inside. Or charge for every use.
Raising prices is loud. People notice a number going up.
Charging per use is scary. Nobody likes a meter running.
So most chose the quietest option. Keep the price. Shrink the box.
However, for most people, almost nothing changes. If you ask a few questions a day, you'll probably never hit a limit.
The squeeze falls on the heaviest users. The ones who let agents work through the night.
And that group is growing every month.
So, was twenty dollars a lie?
Not exactly. The price on the page was always true.
The lie was a word nobody printed, but we all heard anyway.
Unlimited.
Today, an agent working for you can cost more than you pay for it. Soon, agents may hire other agents, all night, on your account.
When that bill arrives, who's going to read the small print?
